name: Survey in Class
description: Zinaida Viktorovna has $$$n$$$ students in her history class. The homework for today included $$$m$$$ topics, but the students had little time to prepare, so $$$i$$$-th student learned only topics from $$$l_i$$$ to $$$r_i$$$ inclusive. At the beginning of the lesson, each student holds their hand at $$$0$$$. The teacher wants to ask some topics. It goes like this: The teacher asks the topic $$$k$$$. If the student has learned topic $$$k$$$, then he raises his hand by $$$1$$$, otherwise he lower it by $$$1$$$. Each topic Zinaida Viktorovna can ask no more than one time . Find the maximum difference of the heights of the highest and the lowest hand that can be in class after the survey. Note that the student's hand can go below $$$0$$$ .
input_specification: Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases $$$t$$$ ($$$1 \le t \le 10^4$$$). The description of the test cases follows. The first line of each test case contains two integers $$$n$$$ and $$$m$$$ ($$$2 \le n \le 10^5, 1 \le m \le 10^9$$$) — the number of students and the number of topics, respectively. Each of the next $$$n$$$ lines of each test case contain two integers $$$l_i$$$ and $$$r_i$$$ ($$$1 \le l_i \le r_i \le m$$$) — the endpoints of the segment of topics that $$$i$$$-th student has learned. It is guaranteed that the sum of $$$n$$$ over all test cases does not exceed $$$10^5$$$.
output_specification: For each test case, print one integer — the maximum difference of the heights of the highest and the lowest hand that can be in the class after the survey.
approach_summary: Build a Segment Tree over the array. Implement point update and associative range query operations in O(log N) time per query.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 1834D — Survey in Class [57. Segment Tree (Point Update Range Query)]
topic_editorial.summary: Range queries and updates via Segment Tree.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: The query operation is associative (e.g., sum, min, max, gcd). Any contiguous range $[L, R]$ can be decomposed into at most $O(\log N)$ canonical dyadic intervals represented by nodes in a binary tree.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Tree Construction
We build a binary segment tree over array $A[1..N]$.
Each node covers a segment $[L, R]$. If $L = R$, the node stores $A[L]$. Otherwise:
$$\text{node.val} = \text{combine}(\text{left\_child.val}, \text{right\_child.val})$$

### Step 2: Point / Range Updates
To update position $pos$ with value $val$:
- Traverse down to the leaf node $[pos, pos]$.
- Update leaf value.
- Recompute ancestor values on the way back up in $O(\log N)$ time.

### Step 3: Range Query Processing
To query the associative aggregate on range $[qL, qR]$:
- If current segment $[L, R]$ is completely within $[qL, qR]$, return node value.
- If disjoint, return identity element.
- Otherwise, split and return $\text{combine}(\text{query}(left), \text{query}(right))$.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((N + Q) \log N)$
  Building the segment tree takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$. Each point/range query and update traverses at most $4 \log N$ tree nodes, requiring $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ time per query.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  A standard binary segment tree requires at most $4N$ nodes to represent elements up to index $N$.
